To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
cochlear sensory stem/progenitor cell populations initially give birth to spheres of different morphologies, which are accompanied by different levels of stemness.
cochlear sensory progenitor cells give rise to spheres with distinct morphologies and features.

cochlear sensory cell-derived spheres consist of morphologically distinct types, which differ in their ability to form spheres, and that solid sphere cells are more likely to give rise to hair cells than other sphere cell types.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the most suitable sphere types for cell-based assays aimed at development of a cell replacement therapy for hearing loss.
the identification of the cochlear sensory epithelial stem cells and their progeny.
the development of new therapies for hearing disorders and deafness.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
cochlear sensory progenitors can be isolated and expanded, but their self-renewal potential and differentiation capacity depend on the sphere morphology and the sphere type.
the sphere formation capacity of cochlear sensory epithelial cells is heterogeneous, consisting of at least three morphologically distinct sphere populations.
the stem cell population in the mouse cochlea is heterogeneous and consists of multiple stem cell types with distinct properties and regenerative capacities.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
solid spheres, and not hollow spheres, are the most appropriate source for stem/progenitor cell populations for hair cell regeneration.
solid spheres derived from mouse cochlea sensory epithelium have self-renewal capacity and are able to differentiate into hair cell-like cells.
the stem cells in the cochlea are heterogeneous, and that they can be isolated from different sources and at different stages of the development.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the sphere population is highly heterogeneous and that the most suitable sphere for hair cell replacement therapies is the solid type.
the sphere population obtained from cochlear sensory epithelial cells is heterogeneous.
the cochlear sensory epithelial stem cell pool, which has been isolated from neonatal mouse and human cochleae, is heterogeneous.
